title: Open Weights

post.author: u/cloudy_dome_jemima
post.title: I'm the volunteer astronomer at a public observatory. Thirty days ago our assistant moved to "a free model on our own server". At 01:10 the first bill came.

blocks.text: I'm Jemima, the volunteer astronomer at Skirlaw Observatory, and its treasurer, since nobody else wanted the job. We're open every day from 16:00 to midnight. Wednesday is open night, when anyone can look through the big telescope. Tonight, Wednesday 30 September, the cloud never broke, so after closing I stayed on with the accounts.

While we're open, visitors ask our assistant questions on screens in the hall and on our website: when's the next open night, what's that bright star. About 600 a day. A language model writes the answers: a program that learned to write by reading huge amounts of text.

A model reads and writes text in small pieces, often part of a word, like tiles in a word game. The pieces are called tokens. One question, sent with our standing instructions and a few pages about the observatory, plus its answer, comes to about 2,000 tokens.

Until the end of August we used a provider's service: a company runs its own model on its own computers and charges for every token. Ours charged $2 per million. 600 questions is 1.2 million tokens a day: $2.40 a day, $72 in a 30-day month, $0.004 an answer. The trustees set aside $100 a month.

Then Asbjorn, our volunteer for the computers, found open models. A model is a big file of learned numbers, called its weights. Some makers publish that file so anyone can download and run it, like a recipe printed in a book instead of a dish you can only order at the restaurant. Those are open-weights models, open models for short.

Just after midnight on Tuesday 1 September he moved the assistant to one, Meta's Llama 3. It runs on a graphics card, a chip built for heavy number work, rented by the hour. "A free model on our own server," he told the trustees: his name for the rented computer the card sits in. The card is $1.00 an hour, answering or not, on all day. A dollar an hour sounded like nothing.
Every model comes with its maker's conditions for using it, like the small print on a hire agreement. That's its licence. Asbjorn says open means free.

The rental company bills each month's hours in one go, just after midnight on the 1st. When he opened the account, I turned on its budget email: a warning sent when a month's charges pass $100. September had no charges at all.
At 01:10 it came. Each line below shows the time, what sent it, and what it said.

01:05  billing       september: 720 hours at $1.00 an hour, $720.00 charged.
01:10  budget email  charges so far in october: $720.00. your budget: $100.00 a month.
The month we went free, each answer cost ten times more.

Same 600 questions a day, 18,000 in September. $720 ÷ 18,000 is $0.04 an answer, against $0.004 on the service. The rental page says the card can answer about 20 questions a minute. Spread over its 24 hours, ours got about 0.4 a minute: busy 2% of the time.

blocks.label: skirlaw_1_oct.png

diagram.aria: Jemima's drawing. Top row, before Wednesday 30 September: the provider's service to the end of August, $72 a month; the move on Tuesday 1 September to an open model, Llama 3, on our own server; the rented card at $1.00 an hour, on all day; 600 questions a day, 2,000 tokens each, only while open. Bottom row, the night: the bill at 01:05, 720 hours at $1.00, $720 charged; the budget email at 01:10, budget $100 a month; per answer, $0.004 on the service and $0.04 on the card; the card busy 2%, able to answer 20 a minute and getting about 0.4. A note gives 18,000 answers in September, $720 divided by 18,000, $0.04 each.

Top: the provider's service until the end of August, $72 a month; the move just after midnight on Tuesday 1 September to Llama 3 on a rented card at $1.00 an hour, on all day; 600 questions a day, all while we're open. Bottom: September's 720 hours charged at 01:05, the budget email at 01:10, $0.04 an answer against $0.004, and a card busy 2% of the time.

blocks.text: Asbjorn says the bill will look better once we use the card more. The trustees meet on Saturday 3 October. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing at Skirlaw is haunted. Your card did what it was rented to do: wait, by the hour. There are three ways to run a model like yours for visitors, called hosting options. A provider's service runs its own model and charges per token. Some companies run the same open models on their own cards and charge per token too. Or you rent or buy a card and run the model yourself, called self-hosting, and pay for every hour, busy or idle. Two questions. How many answers a month would your card need before each one costs no more than on the service? And besides the bill, what did the move change for you?

replies.author: u/cloudy_dome_jemima
replies.text: The point where both cost the same per answer is the card's break-even: $720 ÷ $0.004 = 180,000 answers a month, 6,000 a day. We get 600. Nothing else changed: the same questions, the same kind of answers, and nothing visitors ask is private.

comments.author: u/our_own_card_asbjorn
comments.text: The model is free and the card is ours; paying per token is paying rent forever. Banks and hospitals run their own for a reason: data rules, set by a law or a contract, that say some data must stay in-house, on machines they control. And nobody can change or withdraw the model under them. If $720 is the price, put the bigger Llama 3 on a bigger card, $2.00 an hour, and get our money's worth.

replies.author: u/our_own_card_asbjorn
replies.text: It's open; that's the whole point. I'm no lawyer and this isn't legal advice, but open means free.

comments.author: u/locks_up_waltraud
comments.text: I lock the doors at midnight, and nobody asks the assistant anything until we open at 16:00. Switch the card off when we close and back on when the first question comes: 8 hours a day instead of 24, a third of the bill.

replies.author: u/cloudy_dome_jemima
replies.text: Asbjorn says a timer can do that. After the card is switched on, the model takes about 3 minutes to be copied onto it, so the first question each day waits.

reply.prompt: The trustees meet on Saturday 3 October. What should Skirlaw change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Pay per token until volume or data rules justify a card of its own.
options.part2: On Saturday 3 October the trustees agreed, with one step first. I read Llama 3's licence page and wrote down what it says, with the date and the link. That page says a licensee whose products or services had more than 700 million monthly active users in the calendar month before its release date must request a licence from Meta, and it asks for “Built with Meta Llama 3” to be shown prominently on a related website. The trustees chose to add that line to the assistant's page and filed the note. This is what the page says, not legal advice. On Sunday 4 October Asbjorn moved the assistant to a company that runs the same open model and charges $2 per million tokens, and switched the card off. In the sim: $72 for a 30-day month, $2.40 a day, $0.004 an answer, the same as the old service. We also wrote down when to look again: if questions near 6,000 a day, the card's break-even, or if we ever hold data that must stay in-house.
options.senior: Compare the cost of one answer, not the price tag. A card costs the same every hour, busy or idle, so it only pays once steady volume passes its break-even: 6,000 a day here, against 600. Self-host for high steady volume, data that must stay in-house, or full control. And before any open model goes live, write down what its licence page says, with the date.

options.text: Run the bigger open model on a bigger card, so the money is well spent.
options.verdict: A bigger bill for the same idle hours
options.part2: On Saturday the trustees approved the bigger Llama 3 on a bigger card at $2.00 an hour, on all day, from Monday 5 October. In the sim a 30-day month costs $1,440: $0.08 an answer, 20 times the service. Visitors asked the same 600 questions a day about opening times and the next open night. The bigger card can answer about 10 a minute and got about 0.4, busy 4% of the time. Its break-even rose to 360,000 answers a month, 12,000 a day. Nobody read the licence page.
options.senior: The card was never short of work it could do: it waited 98% of the time. A bigger model fills the same idle hours with a bigger hourly price, so the cost of each answer doubles. Spending more so the hours feel used only raises the bill.

options.text: Keep the card: an open model is free to use, with no conditions attached.
options.verdict: Free to download, not to run
options.part2: We kept the card on all day. In the sim every 30-day month repeats September: $720, $0.04 an answer, 10 times the service, busy 2% of the time. In November a visitor asked what our assistant's page should say it was built with. I read the licence page at last. That page says a licensee whose products or services had more than 700 million monthly active users in the calendar month before its release date must request a licence from Meta, and it asks for “Built with Meta Llama 3” to be shown prominently on a related website. Our page showed nothing, and we had no record of which terms we had read or when. Open weights let us download the model; the conditions were on a page nobody had opened. This is what the page says, not legal advice.
options.senior: Open weights means you can download and run the model; the licence page says on what conditions. Licences differ from model to model, and some ask for things a small team easily misses. Read it and write down what it says, with a date, before you rely on it. And free to download is not free to run: the card bills every hour.

options.text: Switch the card off whenever the observatory is closed to its visitors.
options.verdict: A third of the bill, still 3.3 times
options.part2: From Thursday 8 October a timer switched the card off at midnight, and the first question after 16:00 switched it back on. In the sim, 8 hours a day: $240 for a 30-day month, $0.013 an answer, 3.3 times the service, busy 6% of its hours. Every afternoon the first visitor's question waited about 3 minutes while the model was copied onto the card, and some walked off before the answer came. The break-even fell to 60,000 answers a month, 2,000 a day, still more than three times what we get. Nobody read the licence page.
options.senior: Switching off idle hours is a real saving, but $240 is still 3.3 times the service, and the first visitor each day pays for it in waiting. It trims the bill without asking whether a card of your own makes sense at 600 questions a day.

sim.title: Cost the assistant at Skirlaw
sim.lede: You're Jemima at 00:30 on Thursday 1 October, before the bill. No real model runs here: every figure is worked out from given numbers. Given: 600 questions a day, all while the observatory is open, 16:00 to midnight; about 2,000 tokens each; months of 30 days. The provider's service, and a company running the same open model, each charge $2 per million tokens. The rented card costs $1.00 an hour and can answer about 20 questions a minute; the bigger model needs a bigger card at $2.00 an hour that can answer about 10 a minute. After the card is switched on, the model takes about 3 minutes to be copied onto it. The budget is $100 a month. The card has been on all day since 00:00 on Tuesday 1 September.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play the bill: $720 charged, over the $100 budget, and $0.04 an answer, 10 times the service. Switch hosting to the provider's service: $72 a month, $2.40 a day, $0.004 an answer. Back on the card, set questions a day to 6,000, its break-even: $0.004 an answer, the same as the service, busy 21%. Set it back to 600 and run the card 8 hours a day: $240, $0.013, 3.3 times the service, and a wait of about 3 minutes each afternoon. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at Skirlaw was haunted. The open model cost nothing to download, but the card it ran on cost $1.00 every hour, answering or not. At 600 questions a day the card sat waiting 98% of the time, so each answer cost $0.04 instead of $0.004. A card of your own only pays once steady volume passes its break-even, 6,000 a day here, and the model's licence page had conditions nobody had read.

steps.title: What one answer costs, two ways.
steps.text: Per token, the sum runs per question. First, count the tokens: about 2,000. Second, multiply by the price: 2,000 × $2 ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.004. Third, multiply by the questions: 600 a day is $2.40, and a 30-day month $72. On a card, the sum runs per hour. First, count the hours it is on: 24 × 30 = 720. Second, multiply by the hourly price: $720. Third, divide by the answers it gave, 18,000, so $0.04 each. What can go wrong: the card's sum has the answers at the bottom, so fewer questions make every answer dearer, and nobody sees it until the bill.

steps.title: Why the card cost ten times more: it charges for waiting.
steps.text: The card can answer about 20 questions a minute. Spread over its 24 hours, Skirlaw sent it about 0.4 a minute, so it was busy 2% of the time and waiting the other 98%. A provider's service usually shares its cards among many customers and charges only for the tokens you use, so the waiting is spread out and not on your bill. A card of your own bills every hour the same, busy or idle. What can go wrong: switching it off while closed cuts the hours to 8 a day and the bill to $240, but that is still 3.3 times the service, and the first question after each start waits about 3 minutes while the model is copied onto the card.

steps.title: Break-even: when a card of your own pays.
steps.text: Divide the card's month by the service's price for one answer: $720 ÷ $0.004 = 180,000 answers a month, 6,000 a day. Below that, per token is cheaper; above it, the card is, as long as it can keep up: 6,000 a day over 24 hours is about 4.2 a minute, 21% of its 20. A bigger model on a $2.00 card doubles the break-even to 360,000 a month. What can go wrong: volume only counts if it is steady. A card rented for a busy month keeps billing through a quiet one.

steps.title: Open weights come with a licence.
steps.text: Open weights means the maker published the model's file, so you can download it and run it yourself. The licence page says on what conditions. Meta's Llama 3 page says a licensee whose products or services had more than 700 million monthly active users in the calendar month before the release date must request a licence from Meta, and asks for “Built with Meta Llama 3” to be shown. The Apache License, Version 2.0, a general software licence, lists conditions too, such as giving anyone you pass the work on to a copy of the licence. So, before going live: first read the page, then write down what it says with the date and link, then keep the downloaded file pinned by its checksum (a7e06). What can go wrong: licences differ from model to model, and a new version can come with a new page. This is not legal advice.

steps.title: When to self-host.
steps.text: Three reasons usually justify a card of your own. High, steady volume above the break-even. Data that must stay in-house, because a law or a contract says it may not leave machines you control. Or full control: fine-tuning your own copy (a8e02), or keeping one exact version pinned so nobody changes it under you (a6e09). Skirlaw had none of the three: 600 questions a day, nothing private, and no need to change the model. A middle path keeps the open model but pays per token, through a company that runs it. What can go wrong: a card of your own also needs someone to run it, update it and restart it, and Asbjorn is a volunteer.

diagram.aria: The fix. Top row: read the licence page and write it down, dated, with the link; pay per token, $2 a million tokens, $72 a month; count the volume, 600 a day against a break-even of 6,000; stay per token, $0.004 an answer, while below the break-even. Bottom row, self-host only when one of these holds: steady volume past 6,000 a day; data rules that say the data must stay in-house, none at Skirlaw; full control, an own copy pinned, not needed now; then a card, with the licence re-read and its busy share watched.

notes.text: Before going live, and again whenever volume or rules change
Self-host only when one of these holds:

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right: the licence page is read and written down first, the assistant pays per token, and the volume is counted against the card's break-even; below it, it stays per token. Bottom row: only steady volume past 6,000 a day, a data rule that keeps data in-house, or a need for full control makes a card of its own worth it, and then the licence is read again and the card's busy share watched.

fix.title: The fix: write down the licence, pay per token, and say in advance what would justify a card
fix.text: Read the model's licence page and write down what it says, with the date and the link, before anyone relies on it; this is not legal advice, and anything unclear goes to someone qualified. Pay per token while the volume is low: at Skirlaw, the same open model through a company that charges $2 per million tokens, $72 for a 30-day month, $0.004 an answer. Work out the card's break-even, $720 ÷ $0.004 = 180,000 answers a month, 6,000 a day, and write down what would change the answer: steady volume near that, data that must stay in-house, or a need for full control. Then switch the card off.

limits: Break-even assumes today's prices. Per-token prices and card prices both change, so the sum needs doing again when either does.
Paying per token puts the questions on someone else's computers. If a rule later says the data must stay in-house, that settles it whatever the cost.
A dated note of what a licence page says is a record, not legal advice. Whether a condition applies to your use is a question for someone qualified.

explain.seniorTake: Open weights change who may run a model, not what running it costs. A provider's service usually spreads its cards across many customers and charges you only for tokens; a card of your own charges the same every hour, busy or idle, so its cost per answer is the hourly price divided by how much you use it. That makes the decision a sum before it is a preference: the card's monthly cost divided by one answer's per-token cost is its break-even, and below it, per token wins. Self-host when volume is high and steady past that line, when a law or contract says the data must stay in-house, or when you need full control of your own copy, and count the people who will run it. A middle path keeps the open model and pays per token through a company that runs it. Whichever you choose, read the model's licence page and write down what it says, with the date, because open describes the file, and the licence describes the conditions.

realWorld.title: Apache License, Version 2.0: no charge, with conditions
realWorld.text: The Apache Software Foundation's licence page grants a perpetual, worldwide, non-exclusive, no-charge, royalty-free, irrevocable copyright license, and then, for passing the work on, adds: provided that You meet the following conditions. The first reads: You must give any other recipients of the Work or Derivative Works a copy of this License. No charge is not the same as no conditions. This is what the page says, not legal advice.

realWorld.title: Meta Llama 3 licence: the release date and the 700 million line
realWorld.text: Meta's licence page gives Meta Llama 3 Version Release Date: April 18, 2024. Under Additional Commercial Terms it says that if, on that date, the monthly active users of the products or services made available by or for Licensee, or Licensee’s affiliates, is greater than 700 million monthly active users in the preceding calendar month, you must request a license from Meta. Few organisations are that size, but the condition is there to be read. Not legal advice.

realWorld.title: Meta Llama 3 licence: an attribution line
realWorld.text: In its section on redistribution and use, the same page asks to prominently display “Built with Meta Llama 3” on a related website, user interface, blogpost, about page, or product documentation. Whether that applies to a given use is a question for someone qualified; the page is where to start, and a dated copy of what it said is the record.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.32: intellectual property rights
realWorld.text: A third-party guide says Annex A control 5.32 describes the steps organisations need to take to ensure compliance with intellectual property (IP) rights. A model's licence sets such rights, so a dated record of each licence page is the kind of step the control looks for. The wording is the guide's, not the standard's; check the control in your own copy.

realWorld.title: SOC 2 CC9.2: vendors and business partners
realWorld.text: A third-party summary gives criterion CC9.2 as: The entity assesses and manages risks associated with vendors and business partners. A provider's service, or a company that runs an open model for you per token, is such a vendor.

asked: When would you self-host an open model instead of calling an API?
What do you check before using an open-weights model commercially?
interview.answer: I start with the cost of one answer, not the price tag. Per token, it's the tokens per request times the price. On a card it's the hourly price times the hours it runs, divided by the answers it gives, so idle hours raise the cost of every answer. The break-even is the card's monthly cost divided by one answer's per-token cost; below it, an API is cheaper. Then I'd self-host only for one of three reasons: high, steady volume above that break-even, within what the card can keep up with at the busiest hour; data that must stay in-house because a law or contract says so; or full control, such as fine-tuning my own copy or pinning one exact version. I'd count the people cost too: someone has to run, update and restart it, and the first request after a restart waits while the model is copied onto the card. A middle path is a company that runs the same open model and charges per token. Before using any open-weights model commercially, I read its licence page and record what it says, with the date: who may use it, any user-count lines, any attribution it asks for, and the conditions for passing it on. I pin the downloaded file by its checksum. I'm not a lawyer, so anything unclear goes to someone qualified. If the company works to ISO/IEC 27001 or reports against SOC 2, the licence record and the vendor review are part of the evidence.

terms.def: Someone who gives their time, unpaid, to run an observatory's telescopes and talk to visitors. Jemima is Skirlaw's, and its treasurer.
The public observatory in this case, open every day from 16:00 to midnight. Wednesday is open night.
An evening when a public observatory lets anyone look through its big telescope. Skirlaw's is on Wednesdays; on 30 September the cloud never broke.
The people who run a charity such as Skirlaw and decide what it spends. They set aside $100 a month for the assistant.
Skirlaw's program that answers visitors' questions on screens in the hall and on its website while the observatory is open: about 600 a day.
A program that learned to write by reading huge amounts of text, like a phone's next-word suggestions grown very large (a1e01).
A small piece of text, often part of a word, like a tile in a word game. Models read and write in tokens, and per-token prices count them (a1e03).
The text sent with every question telling the model what to do and how, also called the system prompt (a2e01).
A company that runs models on its own computers and sells their use, billed by the token (a6e04).
A provider's model offered for use over the internet and charged per token. Skirlaw's old one charged $2 per million tokens: $0.004 an answer.
Charged by the number of tokens sent and written, so you pay only for what you use. Skirlaw's price: $2 per million.
The learned numbers a model is made of, stored in one big file. Training sets them; running the model uses them (a1e02).
A model whose maker publishes its weights, so anyone can download and run it, like a recipe printed in a book. Also called an open model (a1e08).
Short for open-weights model. Open means the file is published; the model's licence page says on what conditions it may be used.
Meta's family of open-weights language models, released on 18 April 2024 (a1e08). Skirlaw ran one on its rented card from 1 September.
A chip built for heavy number work, also called a GPU (a2e08, a8e02). Skirlaw's rented one cost $1.00 an hour and could answer about 20 questions a minute.
A computer that runs a program for others to use. Asbjorn's word for the rented computer Skirlaw's card sits in.
A maker's written conditions for using what it made, like the small print on a hire agreement. Each open model has its own licence page.
What a licence asks of the people who use the thing, such as showing a line or passing on a copy of the licence.
The company Skirlaw rents its graphics card from by the hour. It bills each month's hours in one go, just after midnight on the 1st.
A warning the rental company sends when a month's charges pass a set amount. Jemima set it at $100; it came at 01:10 on Thursday 1 October.
A month's cost divided by the answers given. At Skirlaw, $0.004 an answer when paid per token; on the card all day, $720 ÷ 18,000 = $0.04 (a6e04).
How much of its time a card spends answering. Skirlaw's could answer about 20 questions a minute and got about 0.4: busy 2%.
Switched on but doing nothing. A rented card bills idle hours at the same price as busy ones.
The ways to run a model for others to use: a provider's service, a company running an open model per token, or a card of your own.
Running a model on a card or computer you rent or own, paying by the hour, rather than paying per token (a2e08).
The volume at which two ways cost the same per answer. Skirlaw's card: $720 ÷ $0.004 = 180,000 answers a month, 6,000 a day.
Rules, set by a law or a contract, that say some data must stay in-house, on machines you control.
On machines you run or control yourself, rather than on a provider's.
Being able to change, fine-tune or pin your own copy of a model, with nobody able to change or withdraw it under you.
After a card is switched on, the model must be copied onto it before it can answer: about 3 minutes at Skirlaw, paid by the first question.
The number of different people who use a product in a month. Meta's Llama 3 licence page draws a line at 700 million.
A short line saying what something was built with. Meta's Llama 3 licence page asks for “Built with Meta Llama 3” to be shown.
A short string worked out from every part of a file, like a fingerprint. A matching checksum means the same file (a7e06).
Tied to one exact file or version, so it changes only when a person moves the pin (a6e09, a7e06).
Training a finished model a little more on your own examples, like altering a suit instead of buying a new one (a8e02).
Short for application programming interface: the way one program asks another for something. Calling a provider's API means sending requests to its service (a2e01).
A general licence from the Apache Software Foundation, dated January 2004. It grants wide rights at no charge and lists conditions for passing the work on.
The international standard for information security management. Its Annex A control 5.32 covers intellectual property rights.
An auditor's report on a company's controls (a7e06). Criterion CC9.2 covers risks from vendors and business partners.
The course's hands-on builds. L8 and N7 cost a loadout per 1,000 checks; the Nightwatch copilot's X6 compares a small self-hosted model with an API model.

atWork: Look for a team that self-hosts an open model to save money at low volume. It is a common pattern: someone sees that the model is free to download, rents a graphics card, and the first month's bill arrives in one lump, often several times what paying per token cost. Ask four things. What does one answer cost each way, and what is the card's break-even? Is the volume steady and above it, and can the card keep up at the busiest hour? Is there a data rule, or a need for full control, that paying per token can't meet? And is each model's licence page read, written down with the date, and on record, with the downloaded file pinned by its checksum? Build Night: L8 and N7 (cheapest loadout, cost per 1,000 checks) use the same arithmetic: the hourly price times the hours, divided by the work done. The Nightwatch copilot's X6 reuses this case: compare a small self-hosted model with an API model on cost per 1,000 answers and on accuracy. Standards-readiness note, not legal advice: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control 5.32 (intellectual property rights, as summarised by third-party guides; check the control in your own copy) is likely to expect each model's licence to be on record. If you report against SOC 2 and use a provider's service, or a company that runs the model for you, criterion CC9.2 (vendor and business partner risk) asks for that vendor's risks to be assessed and managed. A dated licence note and a vendor review cost little now and a lot to reconstruct at audit time.

recall.prompt: A startup's support bot answers about 3,000 questions a day, about 1,500 tokens each, through a provider at $3 per million tokens. An engineer wants to rent a graphics card at $1.50 an hour, on all day, to run an open model, because the model is free. What would you check before agreeing?

keyIdeas.idea: Compare the cost of one answer each way and work out the card's break-even
A card costs the same every hour, busy or idle, so low volume makes each answer dearer
Self-host only for steady volume above the break-even, data that must stay in-house, or full control
Read the model's licence page and record what it says, with the date

recall.model: First the sum, both ways. Per token, one answer is 1,500 × $3 ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.0045, about $405 for a 30-day month. The card is $1.50 × 24 × 30 = $1,080 a month whether it is busy or idle, which over 90,000 answers is $0.012 per answer, more than twice as much. Its break-even is $1,080 ÷ $0.0045 = 240,000 answers a month, 8,000 a day, and we get 3,000. So I'd stay per token unless there is steady volume above that, data that must stay in-house, or a need for full control. And free to download isn't free of conditions: I'd read the model's licence page and record what it says, with the date, before anyone relies on it.

recall.prompt: Skirlaw's card costs $720 for a 30-day month. On the provider's service one answer costs $0.004. How many answers a month would the card need before each one costs no more than on the service?
recall.why: $720 ÷ $0.004 = 180,000 answers a month, which is 6,000 a day. Skirlaw gets 18,000 a month, a tenth of that, so each answer on the card cost ten times as much.

recall.prompt: An interviewer asks: when would you self-host an open model instead of calling an API?

keyIdeas.idea: High, steady volume above the card's break-even, because idle hours cost the same
Data that must stay in-house because a law or contract says so
Full control: fine-tuning your own copy or pinning one exact version

recall.model: When one of three things holds. First, high, steady volume above the break-even: the card's monthly cost divided by what one answer costs per token. Below that, idle hours make every answer dearer. Second, data that must stay in-house because a law or a contract says so. Third, full control: fine-tuning my own copy, or keeping one exact version pinned. Otherwise I'd call an API, or a company that runs the same open model per token, and record the model's licence page either way.

recall.prompt: Meta's Llama 3 licence page names a size above which a licensee must request a licence from Meta. As that page states it, what is the size?
options: More than 700 million monthly active users in the calendar month before the release date
More than 700 million downloads of the model
More than 700 employees on the release date
Any paid use of the model at all
recall.why: That page says that if, on the release date, 18 April 2024, the monthly active users of the licensee's products or services were greater than 700 million in the preceding calendar month, it must request a licence from Meta. It also asks for an attribution line. This is what the page says, not legal advice.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. We've paid per token since October: $72 a month. Now the county wants the assistant in its schools for astronomy lessons, and expects about 9,000 questions a day, all in the school day, 09:00 to 17:00. The county's contract says pupils' questions may not leave machines we or the county control. Asbjorn says: told you, time for a card.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Should Skirlaw move the assistant to a card of its own now, and what should it check first?

keyIdeas.idea: Volume is now past the card's break-even, so per token would cost more
The contract is a data rule that a per-token company may not meet
Check the card can keep up at the busiest hour
Read the licence page again for the new use and record it

coldCase.model: This time the sum and the rules both point to a card. Per token, 9,000 a day is $36 a day, $1,080 for a 30-day month, against $720 for the card on all day: we're past the break-even of 6,000 a day, so the card is cheaper. And the county's contract is a data rule: pupils' questions must stay on machines we control, which a per-token company may not meet. Before switching, two checks. Can the card keep up? If the questions come in an 8-hour school day, 9,000 is nearly 19 a minute against the card's 20, so the busiest hour needs a second card or a queue. And read the licence page again for this new use, write down what it says with the date, and pin the downloaded file by its checksum.
